content_voiceover: Two more high-yield questions on ALL statements and blinatumomab. The first asks which statements are wrong, and the answer is A, meaning statements one and four. Statement one is wrong because early T-cell precursor ALL actually carries a relatively poor prognosis, not a good one. Statement four is wrong because blinatumomab is a bispecific antibody that binds CD3 on T lymphocytes and CD19, not CD20, on the B-cell leukemia blasts. Statements two and three are true, co-expression of lymphoid and myeloid antigens tends to favor ALL-type treatment regimens, and dose-intensified anthracycline plus high-dose Ara-C can improve complete remission rates and disease-free survival. The second question digs deeper into blinatumomab mechanics, and the wrong statements are one and two, answer D. Blinatumomab is actually a CD19, not CD22, bispecific T-cell engager, correcting statement one. And its half-life is much shorter than twelve hours, which is exactly why it's given as a continuous infusion rather than a twice-daily bolus, correcting statement two. Statements three and four are accurate, cytokine release syndrome can be prevented or managed with steroids and tocilizumab, and hypogammaglobulinemia results from on-target depletion of normal B cells.
keypoints: ETP-ALL prognosis is POOR, not good
Blinatumomab targets CD19/CD3, not CD20 or CD22
Blinatumomab has a short half-life, given as continuous infusion (not twice-daily bolus)
CRS managed with steroids +/- tocilizumab; hypogammaglobulinemia from B-cell depletion
keypoint_voiceover: Two blinatumomab traps to memorize, it targets CD19 and CD3, never CD20 or CD22, and its short half-life means it's delivered as a continuous infusion, not a twice-daily bolus. Also lock in that ETP-ALL has a poor, not favorable, prognosis, that's a recurring board distractor.
